fact: A use case represents how a system interacts with its environment by illustrating the activities performed by the users of the system and the system's responses
Use cases are regarded as an EXTERNAL or FUNCTIONAL perspective on a business process, showing how users interact with it rather than its internal procedures or technical details

The importance of use cases: they identify and clarify functional requirements, and a well-developed use case diagram captures most of the system's functional requirements; they are very helpful in understanding exceptions, special cases and error handling that developers easily overlook; and the text-based use case narrative is easy for users to understand while flowing easily into the process model and the data model
USE-CASE MODELLING is the process of modelling a system's functions in terms of business events, who initiates them, and how the system responds to them
Use-case modelling has TWO primary outputs: the use case DIAGRAM and the use case NARRATIVE

A use-case diagram graphically depicts the system as a collection of use cases, actors and their relationships, giving a high-level view of the business events the system must process, showing who will use the system and how users expect to interact with it

A use case documents the interaction required between the user and the system to accomplish the user's task; use cases can also be referred to as system activities, and are represented by an ELLIPSE with the name written inside

Use cases are triggered by external users called ACTORS; actors are ALWAYS OUTSIDE the system boundary and initiate or participate in use cases by sending inputs to the system or receiving outputs from it, and each actor is defined based on what they do in relation to the system

There are four types of actors. PRIMARY BUSINESS ACTOR primarily benefits from the execution of the use case by receiving something of measurable or observable value, such as an employee receiving a salary. PRIMARY SYSTEM ACTOR directly interfaces with the system to initiate or trigger a business event, such as the bursar who dispenses cash. EXTERNAL SERVER ACTOR responds to a request from the use case, such as the Financial Director approving cash dispensing. EXTERNAL RECEIVER ACTOR is not the primary actor but receives something of measurable or observable value from the use case, such as a warehouse receiving a packing order

An ASSOCIATION, also called a communication relationship, represents a direct interaction between an actor and a use case, drawn as a simple line; an association WITH an arrowhead touching the use case indicates the use case was initiated by the actor at the other end, while an association WITHOUT an arrowhead indicates an interaction between the use case and an external server or receiver actor

An EXTENDS relationship extracts complex functionality from a use case into its own use case so users can better follow the process; it is optional or conditional behaviour that extends a base use case under specific conditions, and the ARROW IS DRAWN FROM THE EXTENSION TO THE USE CASE BEING EXTENDED

An INCLUDE or USE relationship is used when one use case ALWAYS requires the behaviour of another as part of its execution; the included use case represents common functionality reused by multiple use cases, which promotes reuse and avoids duplication, for example validating a customer both when placing an order and when making a payment

A DEPENDS ON relationship indicates that one use case relies on another for its execution and cannot be performed until the other has been performed; in a bank, withdrawing cash depends on first depositing cash, and depositing cash depends on opening a bank account; a change in one use case may affect the other, which makes it valuable for managing change impact

GENERALISATION or INHERITANCE is used when two or more actors have the same function or behaviour, extracting the shared behaviour into a new ABSTRACT actor; in the bank example Customer is the abstract actor, and Savings Account Holder and Current Account Holder inherit all Customer use cases such as Withdraw Money and Check Balance while having additional specific use cases of their own; it is denoted with a TRIANGLE arrowhead

The SYSTEM BOUNDARY represents the scope of the system, includes the name of the system inside or on top of the diagram, and is a RECTANGLE used to separate the system's internal use cases from external actors

A use-case NARRATIVE is the textual description of a use case, describing how an actor interacts with a system to achieve a specific goal and explaining the sequence of events step by step, without focusing on technical implementation details

The basic elements of a use case narrative are the use case NAME and unique identifier, the ACTORS, the DESCRIPTION or goal, the PRECONDITIONS, the MAIN FLOW or basic flow, the ALTERNATIVE FLOWS or extensions, and the POSTCONDITIONS

PRECONDITIONS are conditions that must be true before the use case begins, and if they are not met the use case cannot proceed; for example to withdraw money a customer must have a valid ATM card and enter a correct PIN

The MAIN FLOW lists the step-by-step sequence of actions between actor and system, describing the ideal scenario where everything works correctly, usually numbered; ALTERNATIVE FLOWS describe variations, exceptions or error situations that branch off the main flow, such as an invalid PIN or insufficient funds; POSTCONDITIONS describe what must be true after the use case completes, such as the account balance being updated

The four steps to produce a requirements use-case model are: identify business actors; identify business requirements and use cases; construct a use-case model diagram; and document the business requirement use-case narrative

Actors should be named with a NOUN or noun phrase; the five questions to find actors are who or what provides input to the system, who or what receives output from the system, are interfaces required for other systems, are there any events automatically triggered at a predetermined time, and who will maintain information in the system

The five questions to find important use cases are: what are the main tasks of the actor, what information does the actor need from the system, what information does the actor provide to the system, does the system need to inform the actor of changes or events, and does the actor need to inform the system of changes or events

A system can be modelled AS-IS, documenting the current state including processes, data flows, rules, users and technologies without introducing assumptions, or TO-BE, representing the desired future state after improvements describing how the system should operate to better support business goals
